content: 1. In a study conducted in New Zealand, fortified milk was provided in identical 17-mL scoops. The milk contained 1 mcg of folic acid, 8 mg of vitamin C, 24 mcg of folic acid, 28 mg of zinc as zinc oxide, and 48 mg of ascorbic acid per 400 mL. Units of 220 g of the product were packaged in metallic foil sachets. The fortified and unfortified milk packages were indistinguishable except for a color-coded band in the upper corner of the sachet. 2. In a study in Chile (Stekel 1986), fortified milk was distributed through community clinics of the National Health Service. The milk contained 15 mg of iron as ferrous sulfate per 100 g of powdered milk. Mothers received 3 kg of milk product per month until their child was 6 months old and 2 kg per month until the child was 24 months old. The mean breastfeeding duration for participant children was 4 months. 3. Another study in Chile (Stekel 1988) used full-fat powdered milk fortified with 15 mg of iron as ferrous sulfate, 100 mg of ascorbic acid, 1500 IU of vitamin A, and 400 IU of vitamin D per 100 g of powder. Children were clinically followed every 15 days by the same group of physicians. Milk was prepared by daycare staff by adding one color-coded capsule (10 mL) to each liter of milk. 4. In the intervention group of a study, milk was fortified with 5 mg of fluoride and 107 CFU/mL of Lactobacillus rhamnosus LB21 per liter. Capsules in the control group contained only skimmed milk and were identical in appearance except for the color code. 5. Animal milk, specified as cow's milk, was used in all trials. Some studies specified the use of full-fat or low-fat cow's milk, pasteurized milk, or semi-skimmed milk. Twelve studies used powdered milk, while two studies did not specify the form of milk used. 6. Follow-on formulas were used in several studies, often provided free of charge. These formulas varied in micronutrient concentrations and were sometimes fortified with additional components such as short-chain galacto-oligosaccharides, polyunsaturated fatty acids, prebiotics, and probiotics. 7. Fortified milk was provided in powder form in five studies and in liquid form in two studies. The milk was fortified with multiple micronutrients, including iron, vitamin C, and vitamin D. Iron fortifiers included ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, and ferrous lactate. 8. In one study, fortified milk was prepared daily using single-serve sachets containing fluoride and probiotics. Mothers were advised to feed their children three sachets per day. 9. Funding sources for the studies varied. Eight studies were supported by private industry, while five were funded by academic, governmental, or non-governmental organizations. Some studies declared no financial support from baby food companies, while others did not report funding sources. 10. Declarations of conflicts of interest were inconsistent across studies. Some authors declared no conflicts, while others received grants or support from industry sponsors. Nine studies did not report any declarations of interest. 11. The systematic review included comparisons between animal milk and follow-on formulas. Evidence suggested that follow-on formulas made little or no difference to body weight, height, or other growth parameters compared to animal milk in children aged 12–23 months. 12. Serum vitamin D levels and vitamin D deficiency were reported in two studies, with moderate certainty evidence suggesting no significant differences between animal milk and follow-on formulas. 13. Serum iron levels were reported in one study, with low certainty evidence indicating no significant differences between the two groups. 14. No data were found on long-term food preferences, dietary patterns, or non-communicable disease outcomes in the included studies.
